guideTitle: Best Paper Shredders for Credit Cards (2026)
metaTitle: Best Paper Shredders for Credit Cards (2026)
metaDescription: Six shredders that cut credit cards as well as paper, compared on card handling, cut size, run time and the limits that decide whether a card shreds cleanly.
expertTake: The Bonsaii 12-sheet micro-cut with a 5.5-gallon bin is the best card shredder here because it turns a card and a page into the same fine particles. The Amazon Basics 12-sheet cross-cut is the value pick for a household that only shreds the odd expired card. Skip a paper-focused shredder altogether if you destroy cards in bulk, since a dedicated card cutter handles that better.
introParagraphs: A credit card is a different job from a sheet of paper. It is a stiff plastic slab with a chip and a magnetic stripe, and it asks more of the cutter than any normal page does. Many shredders list card capability, but the real differences show up in how many cards per pass, how fast the motor tires and how small the pieces are.

Buyers often assume that a machine rated for cards will chew through a stack of them. In practice, most home units take one card at a time, ask for a rest afterwards and leave large chunks if the cut type is coarse. The right pick depends on how often cards come through and how much risk you place on a recoverable chip.

products.name: Bonsaii 12-Sheet Micro-Cut Shredder, Cards and Clips, 5.5 Gal
products.description:
A card shredded into micro-cut pieces is the safest outcome, because the chip, stripe and printed number all end up in fragments too small to read. This Bonsaii cuts to P-4 and lists cards, clips and staples among the things it can take, which makes it the most reassuring choice for people who dispose of cards regularly.

The 12-sheet head is about average for a home unit, but the real value is the pairing with a 5.5-gallon bin. Card fragments are heavier than paper confetti, so a bigger bin prevents the awkward moment when a half-full basket jams the cutter head. A patented cooling system supports a 5-minute continuous run, which is enough for a handful of cards plus a stack of statements.

In year three the main chore is the cutter. Plastic leaves a waxy residue, so oiling according to the manual matters more here than on a paper-only machine. Compared with the Amazon Basics 8-sheet micro-cut, you gain four sheets of capacity and a much larger bin. Keep metal-edged cards out of the slot.
products.bestFor: People who dispose of cards often and want the finest fragments.

products.name: Amazon Basics 12-Sheet Cross-Cut Paper and Card Shredder

specList.label: Cards
specList.value: One at a time, no metal

products.description:
This is the simplest route to a machine that handles both paper and plastic. It cuts 12 sheets of 20 lb paper at a time into pieces roughly 5 by 30 millimetres, and also shreds credit cards one at a time. Metal cards are specifically excluded.

Its nine-minute run time is the longest among the Amazon Basics models in this group, and the 30-minute rest after it is typical. Overheat protection shuts the motor off before damage occurs. The cross-cut pieces are longer than micro-cut chips, so security is a notch lower. For most expired cards, that is enough because the chip is destroyed and the number is split across several pieces.

Ownership is easy: empty the bin, keep it clear and watch the thermal stops. If you destroy cards weekly, step up to the Bonsaii micro-cut for finer particles. For a household that does so a few times a year, this unit is the sensible spend and sits a tier below the micro-cut alternatives.

products.name: Amazon Basics 8-Sheet High Security Cross-Cut Card Shredder
products.description:
At 5 by 18 millimetres, the pieces from this model are about 40 percent shorter than those from the 12-sheet Amazon Basics, and it meets P-4. That makes it the more secure of the two Amazon Basics cross-cuts, at the cost of a lower sheet count.

The three-minute run time is the shortest in this guide, and the 30-minute rest afterwards means you cannot shred a big pile at once. Cards go through one at a time, and metal cards are not suitable. The auto shut-off protects the motor if you push past the limit.

It is a tidy desktop unit that rewards small, frequent jobs. If you plan on feeding more than a few cards in a row, expect to pause. Compared with the Bonsaii 6-sheet, it offers two more sheets of capacity but a shorter run, so it is better for paper-and-card mixes than for pure card disposal. Treat it as a compact security upgrade.
products.bestFor: Small desks where P-4 cross-cut security matters and batches are short.

products.name: Amazon Basics 8-Sheet High Security Micro-Cut Card Shredder
products.description:
A micro-cut at 4.5 by 12 millimetres is the strongest answer to the card problem in the Amazon Basics range. It shreds CDs and credit cards as well as paper, and accepts staples and small clips without a sorting step.

The duty cycle is five minutes on and thirty off, which is 67 percent longer on than the 3-minute cross-cut sibling. That extra time is useful when you have a mix of cards and paper. Overheat protection shuts the motor down if you push on. The pull-out bin makes emptying less awkward than lifting the head.

The weakness is capacity. Eight sheets per pass is modest, and micro-cut is slow, so large stacks will take patience. It is not a machine for a full drawer of paperwork. As a cards-and-statements machine for a household, it is a solid value that sits below the Bonsaii micro-cut in price tier but also in bin size. It will serve a kitchen-table workflow well.

products.name: Bonsaii 15-Sheet Cross-Cut Shredder, 10-Minute Run
products.description:
Ten minutes of continuous running is twice the 5-minute cycle of the Bonsaii micro-cut, and the 15-sheet head moves 25 percent more paper per pass. If your card disposal comes bundled with a big stack of old statements, this is the machine that gets through the lot.

The four-mode control gives you Auto, Off, Forward and Reverse, which means you can back out a card that has caught awkwardly instead of fighting it. P-4 cross-cut security is good enough for typical household use, and a transparent window in the bin shows when it needs emptying.

The compromise is the cut. Cross-cut pieces are longer than micro-cut, so a card ends up in larger chunks than it would on the Bonsaii 12-sheet micro-cut. Keep the cutters clean, as plastic leaves a residue. This unit suits families that shred paper heavily and cards only sometimes, and who prefer longer sessions to fine particles.

products.name: Bonsaii 6-Sheet Cross-Cut Shredder for Home, 3.4 Gal
products.description:
The smallest unit in this guide is still a P-4 shredder with cards and staples on its menu. Particles measure about 5 by 14 millimetres, which sits between the two Amazon Basics cross-cut sizes and gives decent protection for a card and a few pages.

Its shred time is four minutes with a 20-minute cooling cycle, the shortest rest of the group. The head has a handle for easy lifting, and the separate 3.4-gallon bin has a window so you can check fullness without opening it. It is intended for a single room or a small apartment.

Ownership is simple but the limits are clear. A 6-sheet capacity makes it a slow tool for paper, and a card-heavy job will hit the four-minute limit quickly. It is the budget option for a household that has a few cards to cut and a little paper. Spend up to the Bonsaii 15-sheet if you want more headroom.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Most home shredders cut cards one at a time, and the Amazon Basics models say so explicitly while excluding metal cards. A dedicated card slot or a manual mode, as on some Bonsaii units, keeps plastic away from the paper feed. Always feed a card square to the opening and never push it with force.

A card in cross-cut pieces can leave chunks large enough to read part of a number, while micro-cut fragments are much smaller. The Bonsaii 12-sheet micro-cut and Amazon Basics micro-cut produce roughly 4.5 to 5 by 12 millimetre bits, against the 5 by 30 of the Amazon Basics 12-sheet cross-cut. For high-value cards, go finer.

Cards load the motor more than paper, so short run times bite quickly. The Amazon Basics 8-sheet cross-cut runs 3 minutes, the Bonsaii 6-sheet 4, the Bonsaii micro-cut 5, the Amazon Basics 12-sheet 9 and the Bonsaii 15-sheet 10. If you feed several cards in a row, favour the longer cycles.

The same machine will also see paper, and capacity decides how patient you must be. An 8-sheet micro-cut is slow with a large stack, while a 15-sheet Bonsaii clears it faster. Buy one step above your usual stack.

Plastic fragments are heavier than paper and fill bins by weight before volume. The Bonsaii micro-cut with a 5.5-gallon bin is more forgiving than the 3.4-gallon bin of the Bonsaii 6-sheet. A window in the bin helps you stop before it overfills.

Plastic leaves a waxy film on the cutters, so oiling matters more on a card shredder than on a paper-only one. Follow the manual's schedule and do not use sprays that are not approved. A dull cutter makes a card jam far more likely.

howWeEvaluated.title: Card handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked how each machine says it treats cards, including whether it limits them to one at a time and whether metal is excluded. The Amazon Basics units are explicit, and the Bonsaii units list cards, clips and staples. Anything unclear lost points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Particle size
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared cut dimensions across the lineup, from 4.5 by 12 millimetres to 5 by 30. Finer particles scored higher for cards. A cross-cut unit with long strips ranked below a micro-cut one for this use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Duty cycle
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed run time against cooldown because cards stress the motor. A 10-minute Bonsaii 15-sheet is far more useful for a mixed pile than a 3-minute Amazon Basics 8-sheet.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership burden
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at bin size, cutter upkeep and ease of emptying. The 5.5-gallon bin on the Bonsaii micro-cut helps with heavy plastic chips. This is based on spec sheets and owner feedback patterns.

howWeEvaluated.title: Paper performance
howWeEvaluated.description: Card shredders still handle paper, so we considered sheet capacity. The spread runs from 6 to 15 sheets, and larger heads rank higher for dual-use buyers.

faq.q: Can any shredder handle credit cards?
faq.a: Only models that list cards among accepted items. Most take one card at a time and exclude metal ones. Always check the manual before feeding. A machine that merely survives a card is not the same as one built for it, and a listing that never mentions cards should be treated as paper only.
Not strictly, but it is safer. A cross-cut leaves longer plastic pieces that can show part of a number. A micro-cut leaves fragments too small to use.
Not if the model is rated for them and you feed one at a time. Plastic dulls cutters faster than paper, so oiling and cooldown breaks matter more.

faq.q: Why does it stop after a few cards?
faq.a: That is the thermal cutoff. Cards load the motor heavily, so short run times of 3 to 5 minutes are reached quickly. Let the unit rest.

faq.q: How many cards can I feed at once?
faq.a: One at a time on most home machines. Feeding two risks a stall and shortens cutter life. Wait for the first card to clear before the next one goes in, and keep the card flat against the guide so it enters square rather than at an angle.

faq.q: Should I cut the chip first?
faq.a: Cutting the chip with scissors before shredding is a cheap extra step if you want added security. It is not required with micro-cut units. Also remember gift cards, loyalty cards and old ID badges, which often carry a stripe or chip worth destroying along with the bank cards.
